Definition of 'Adverse event' (AE):

Any untoward medical occurence, unintended disease or injury or any untoward clinical signs (including an abnormal laboratory finding) in subjects, users or other persons whether or not related to the investigational medical device.

Definition of 'Serious Adverse Event' (SAE):

A SAE is any adverse event that led to any of the following: 

a) death

b) serious deterioration in health of the subject, that resulted in any of the following:

  • life-threatening illness or injury
  • permanent impairment of a body structure or a body function
  • hospitalisation or prolongation of patient hospitalisation
  • medical or surgical intervention to prevent life-threatening illness or injury or permanent impairment to a body structure or a body function,
  • chronic disease

c) foetal distress, foetal death or a congenital physical or mental imparment or birth defect

Any SERIOUS Adverse Event (SAE) must be reported within 24 hours awareness

Legend for severity of (S)AE:

  • Mild: aware of symptoms but easily tolerated
  • Moderate: discomfort causing interference with usual activity
  • Severe: incapacitating with inability to work or to do usual activity 

Guidance for sponsor: any SAE with a causal relationship to the IMD, comparator or procedure should be reported to the CA(s) within strict timelines.

PROTOCOL DEVIATION:

MINOR: A minor protocol deviation occurs when, without significant consequences, the activities on a study diverge from the Ethics Committee (EC)-approved protocol (e.g. missing a routine follow-up visit window because the subject is traveling). A minor deviation does not impact study endpoints, data quality, integrity and/or the rights, safety or well-being of the subject(s) and does not invalidate or compromise the study results. 

MAJOR: A major protocol deviation is defined as a departure from the protocol that materially (a) reduces the quality, integrity or completeness of the data, (b) makes the Informed Consent Form inaccurate or invalid, or (c) impacts a subject' safety, rights, or wellbeing, or (d) has an impact on the study endpoints.
In case of a major protocol deviation, a root cause evaluation must be performed and a CAPA (Corrective Action Preventive Action) plan must be completed and signed.

Examples of major protocol deviations may include the following:

- Inadequate or missing informed consent - Inclusion/exclusion criteria not met 
- Missing/late reporting of serious adverse events
- Improper/unauthorized unblinding
- Use of prohibited medication
- Incorrect or missing tests (in case critical tests are linked to eligibility or primary endpoint)
- Mishandled samples which may compromise subject eligibility or primary study/safety endpoints
- Multiple missed or out of window visits
- Intentional departure from protocol
- Repeated non-compliance with study requirements (as such, the accumulation of recurring and/or systematic minor protocol deviations, may be qualified as a major protocol deviation)
